notes.reason: The claim is clearly Masley's own: he writes about "buildings optimized down to the literal atom that will collectively take up about a third of the land we currently use to grow Christmas trees", and he is defending that figure, not reporting someone else's. The note is factually right. I fetched his linked land use article and both accepted quotes are verbatim: it says "By 2030, data center buildings themselves will take up 1/15th of the land area we use to grow Christmas trees" and "1,400 square miles is about 3.5 squares here, 3.5x as much as the land we currently dedicate to Christmas trees". So the number he gives here is about five times his own published figure for buildings, and no figure in that article is a third. What gives me pause is whether the correction matters. The error runs against his own argument, because the real figure is smaller and makes the "not enough land" worry look even sillier, and a reader takes away the same conclusion either way. So this reads as correcting a slip rather than correcting a belief, and Masley may find it beside the point even though he would probably agree it is a slip. One smaller risk: the extracted claim line drops the word "buildings" and says "all proposed and planned data centers", for which his own figure is 3.5x, not a third. The note text itself says "data center buildings" and is fine, but anyone reading the claim line alone could be misled.
